quests.persona: a colleague who takes credit in a way that's ambiguous, possibly unintentional
quests.scene: In a meeting, a colleague says: 'I've been working on improving our onboarding process,' referring to something you both worked on together, with you doing the bulk of the actual redesign.
options: Right, admittedly, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, so there might be a better way to handle it — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
Actually, I did most of that work, not just 'we.', thinking about it now, I hadn't weighed all the details, so feel free to push back.
Yeah, we've been working on it together — I've mainly focused on the redesign side, and Priya's handled the documentation piece.
quests.hint: When your contribution is understated, possibly unintentionally, calmly adding the accurate detail is often better than staying silent or reacting sharply.
quests.explanation: Calmly adding the accurate detail corrects the record without assuming bad intent, which fits a situation that might just be imprecise phrasing. Staying silent lets an inaccurate impression stand, which could affect how your contribution is perceived over time. Reacting sharply assumes the worst about your colleague's intent, when a calmer correction would achieve the same accurate outcome.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that staying silent lets an inaccurate impression about your contribution stand uncorrected.
You may notice that the pointed correction may come across as more confrontational than necessary for what might just be an imprecise, unintentional phrasing.
You calmly add your own contribution to the record, in a way that corrects the impression without accusing anyone of anything.

quests.persona: a coworker whose email summary slightly overstates their role on a shared deliverable
quests.scene: A coworker sends a team-wide email: 'I finished the client onboarding guide,' though you actually wrote half of it and they edited it.
options: Okay, thanks for the update.
Nice work getting that finalized! I'll just add — I drafted the first half and Sam edited it into its final form, in case anyone has questions about specific sections.

That's not really accurate, I wrote half of that myself, to be fair, I hadn't checked how that would actually land, so I could be wrong — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: When a summary understates your role, adding the accurate detail warmly, alongside acknowledging their contribution, works better than staying silent or correcting them sharply in public.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging their contribution while warmly adding your own creates an accurate record without turning it into a public confrontation. Simply thanking them for the update lets your own real contribution go unacknowledged to the team. A direct, corrective reply, sent to the whole team, may feel more confrontational than necessary for what's likely just an imprecise summary.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, letting the slightly overstated summary stand means your own contribution goes unacknowledged to the wider team.
Realistically, you acknowledge their genuine contribution while accurately noting your own, in a friendly, non-confrontational way.
Realistically, the direct correction, sent to the whole team, may feel like more of a public confrontation than the situation actually calls for.

quests.persona: a manager who presents a strategy to the executive team as their own, when it was substantially developed by you and your peer over several months
quests.scene: In an executive presentation, your manager says: 'I developed this go-to-market strategy after analyzing the market landscape,' when in reality, you and a peer did the bulk of the analysis and strategy development together with your manager over several months of collaborative work.
options: This has genuinely been a great collaborative effort — Priya and I did a lot of the market analysis and strategy modeling alongside you over the past few months, and it's exciting to see it land so well with the executive team.
Great presentation.
Actually, Priya and I did most of the actual work on this, not just you.
quests.hint: When a manager overstates their individual role on collaborative work in front of senior leadership, assert the collaborative reality gracefully and factually, rather than staying silent or confronting them pointedly in public.
quests.explanation: Asserting the collaborative reality gracefully, while genuinely celebrating the positive outcome, corrects the record factually without creating unnecessary conflict in front of executives. Staying completely silent, especially in this visible a setting, lets an inaccurate impression stand that could affect how your contributions are seen going forward. A pointed, public correction of your manager, even if the underlying point is fair, risks creating real tension in a high-stakes setting where a calmer approach could achieve the same correction.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you calmly assert the collaborative reality in a way that's factual and gracious, without directly confronting your manager in front of executives.
You may notice that staying silent, especially in front of executives, lets an inaccurate impression about the collaborative effort go completely uncorrected.
As a result, the pointed, public correction of your manager in front of executives is likely to create real tension, even though the underlying point about collaboration is fair.

quests.persona: a coworker asking you to review something with a very tight, somewhat unreasonable turnaround
quests.scene: A coworker says: 'Could you review this 40-page report in the next hour? I know it's a lot, but I really need it before my 3pm.' It's currently 2:00pm.
options: An hour's not enough time to properly review 40 pages — I could do a focused pass on the executive summary and key sections by 3, would that help for your meeting?
Sure, I'll try to get through it.
That's really not enough time for a review like that.
quests.hint: When a deadline is genuinely unrealistic for the full task, propose a scoped-down version that's still genuinely useful within the time available.
quests.explanation: Being honest about the real time constraint, while proposing a scoped, useful alternative, actually helps your coworker within what's realistically possible. Agreeing to the full review risks a rushed job that could miss something important in a document going into a real meeting. Simply saying there's not enough time, without an alternative, doesn't help your coworker with their actual, immediate need.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you're honest about the real constraint while offering a genuinely useful, scoped alternative that still helps within the time available.
As a result, agreeing to an unrealistic timeframe risks a rushed, low-quality review that might miss something important.
Here, the pushback is honest but doesn't offer any alternative that could still genuinely help your coworker before their meeting.

quests.persona: a client asking for a major feature addition with an unreasonable timeline
quests.scene: A client says: 'We need this new integration built and live by next week.' Based on your team's estimation, this realistically takes at least a month.
options: We'll see what we can do.
That timeline just isn't realistic for something like this.
I want to be straight with you — based on our estimates, this realistically needs about a month to build properly. Could we look at a phased rollout, with a basic version live sooner?
quests.hint: When a client's timeline is genuinely unrealistic, be honest about the real estimate and propose a phased or partial alternative.
quests.explanation: Being honest about the real timeline, while proposing a phased alternative, gives the client an accurate picture and a genuine path forward. A vague 'we'll see' doesn't give the client the honest information they need to actually plan around. Flatly saying the timeline isn't realistic, without an alternative, leaves the client without any path forward, even though your underlying assessment is accurate.
consequencePreviews: Here, the vague, non-committal answer doesn't give the client an honest picture of the real timeline they're actually working with.
Realistically, the direct pushback is accurate but doesn't offer the client any alternative path forward that could still meet part of their need.
Realistically, you're honest about the real timeline while proposing a practical, phased solution that could still meet some of the client's urgency.

quests.persona: a hospital administrator asking a clinical team to implement a significant new protocol within an unreasonably short timeframe, citing regulatory pressure
quests.scene: An administrator says: 'Regulatory requires this new protocol live in 48 hours, no exceptions.' Your team believes proper staff training alone requires at least a week to do safely, given the protocol affects patient safety procedures.
options: We'll do our best to get everyone trained in time.

I understand the regulatory pressure, and patient safety matters here too — 48 hours isn't enough for proper training on something this significant. Could we get an extension, or implement a partial, clearly-flagged version while full training completes?
48 hours just isn't enough time for something like this.
quests.hint: When a deadline collides with a genuine risk to people's wellbeing, honestly acknowledge the outside forces driving the timeline while proposing an option that treats both the urgency and the risk as real.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging the regulatory pressure honestly, while proposing a solution that protects patient safety, takes both real constraints seriously rather than picking one over the other. Agreeing to the full timeline risks a genuinely dangerous, rushed implementation of something affecting patient safety. Simply pushing back on the timeline, without an alternative, doesn't help the administrator navigate the genuine regulatory pressure they're also facing.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, agreeing to an unrealistic timeline for something involving patient safety risks a genuinely dangerous rushed implementation.
As a result, you acknowledge the real regulatory pressure while being honest about a genuine patient-safety risk, and you propose a solution that takes both seriously.
Realistically, the direct pushback is accurate but doesn't propose an alternative that could still meet the genuine regulatory pressure your administrator is facing.

quests.persona: your manager during your first performance review, asking for self-assessment
quests.scene: Your manager asks: 'How would you rate your own performance this quarter, and why?' You've had solid results but also know a couple of areas where you could have done better.
options: I think I did pretty well, thinking about it now, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so there might be a better way to handle it — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.

Honestly, I don't think I did that well this quarter, there's a lot I could have done better, admittedly, I said that fairly quickly, though I'm open to changing my mind — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
Overall I'd say strong — I hit all my main targets and the Denholm project went really well. One area I'd like to grow in is delegating more, I noticed I held onto some tasks longer than necessary.
quests.hint: A strong self-assessment names specific real strengths and a specific, genuine area for growth, rather than being vague or overly self-critical.
quests.explanation: Naming specific real strengths and one genuine area for growth gives your manager an honest, useful, and balanced self-assessment. A vague 'pretty well' doesn't give your manager the specific detail that makes a review actually useful. Being overly self-critical, when your results were genuinely solid, undersells your real performance and isn't an accurate reflection either.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, the vague self-assessment doesn't give your manager the specific detail that makes a self-review genuinely useful.
Here, the overly self-critical framing undersells real, solid results, which isn't an accurate or useful self-assessment either.
You give a balanced, honest self-assessment that highlights real strengths and a genuine, specific area for growth.

quests.persona: a client asking for your honest self-assessment of a project you led
quests.scene: A client asks: 'How do you think the project went, looking back?' The project succeeded overall, though there was one significant delay that frustrated the client at the time.
options: I think it went really well overall.

Overall I think it was a success — we hit the key goals. I do think the mid-project delay was a real miss on our part, and I've already put a process in place to catch that kind of thing earlier next time.
Honestly, there were some real problems, especially with that delay.
quests.hint: A candid look back on a finished piece of work with a client names what actually went well and what genuinely fell short, along with the concrete fix already underway.
quests.explanation: Naming the overall success, owning the specific issue honestly, and mentioning a concrete fix gives the client a balanced, trustworthy assessment. Only mentioning the success risks seeming like you're avoiding a real issue the client clearly remembers. Focusing mainly on the problem undersells the project's genuine overall success, which isn't a fully accurate picture either.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, not acknowledging the delay, which genuinely frustrated the client, may come across as avoiding a real issue they clearly remember.
Realistically, you give an honest, balanced assessment that owns the real issue while fairly recognizing the overall success.
Focusing mainly on the problem undersells the project's genuine overall success, which isn't a fully accurate picture either.

quests.persona: a hiring committee asking you to honestly assess your own readiness for a significant promotion
quests.scene: A hiring committee member asks: 'Be honest with us — where do you think you still have gaps for a role at this level?' This is a high-stakes moment where you want to be honest without undermining your own case.
options: Honestly, I think my technical leadership is strong, but I'm still building depth in cross-functional influence at the exec level — it's something I've been actively working on, for example through the cross-team initiative I led last quarter.
I think I'm ready for this role in every way.
Honestly, there are quite a few areas I'm still not confident in.
quests.hint: For a high-stakes self-assessment, honest specificity about a real gap, paired with evidence of active growth, tends to be more persuasive than claiming no gaps or being vaguely self-doubting.
quests.explanation: Naming a specific, genuine gap alongside concrete evidence of active growth shows exactly the kind of self-awareness the committee is looking for, which strengthens rather than weakens your case. Claiming complete readiness with no gaps may actually come across as lacking self-awareness, which many committees specifically watch for. Being vaguely self-critical, without specifics or evidence of growth, undermines your case without giving the committee anything useful to actually evaluate.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, you give a genuinely honest, specific answer that shows self-awareness while demonstrating active growth, which strengthens rather than undermines your case.
Claiming no gaps at all, for a significant promotion, may come across as lacking the self-awareness the committee is specifically testing for.
Realistically, the vague, overly self-doubting answer undermines your case without giving the committee any specific, useful information about genuine growth.
